newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TNT SEES C. EUROPE AUTO PARTS CARGO GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: TNT SEES C. EUROPE AUTO PARTS CARGO GROWTH.

text.p: Express distribution company TNT Express Worldwide said on Thursday its shipments of auto parts from central Europe could reach 160 tonnes a week within five years.
"We now move something like 30-to-40 tonnes a week from automotive parts suppliers in central Europe," Adam Shuter, general manager for TNT's automotive business, told Reuters.
"Five years ago, the volume was zero," he added, speaking by telephone from his office in Northampton in Britain.
"Five years from now, we could easily triple or quadruple our current levels."
Foreign investment will fuel the growth, as major automakers and their suppliers locate operations in the region to take advantage of the low-cost and high-skilled workforce, he said.
"A hugh influx of international suppliers are relocating some operations to former East bloc countries," Shuter said.
"They're clearly doing this for reasons of costs, especially labour costs."
Many of them export finished products back to their home markets, but some also supply privatised automakers in central and eastern Europe, he said.
Nearly 100 foreign suppliers have invested in the Czech Republic, and over 60 of them supply Skoda automobilova AS, a Czech automaker owned 70 percent by German automaker Volkswagen AG .
The bulk of TNT's auto business in the region involves shipping parts to west European plants of U.S. automakers Ford Motor Co and General Motors Corp , Shuter said.
GM already has announced plans to buy $1.0 billion a year in auto parts from the region by 2000, and it opened an office in Warsaw in 1995 to scout new suppliers.
Most of TNT deliveries arrive in Britain and Germany from the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, he said, adding that exports from Poland are relatively small.

Poland has the biggest market for new autos in central Europe with sales topping 428,000 units in 1996, but many of the country's parts manufacturers satisfy their capacity by supplying domestic automakers, Shuter said.
Despite strong demand for auto parts transport, most shipments occur on scheduled deliveries by road, he said, adding that only unusual emergency shipments are by air.
"Emergency air supply is peanuts -- about 500 kilograms a week," he said.

"For every tonne of road freight, we might put 10 kilograms in the air, and we don't expect this to change in central Europe. In the automotive supply business, the use of air freight is usually reserved for making up for mistakes."
TNT's most common parts exports from central Europe include cables, insulation material and pipe bits, Shuter said.

One of the biggest suppliers is the Hungarian plant of U.S. conglomerate United Technologies Corp , which delivers wire harnesses for all Astra cars built by GM's British subsidiary Vauxhall Motors Ltd.

TNT -- wholly owned by the Netherland's private post and telecommunications company Koninklijke PTT Nederland NV-- also expects growing business from a new bus-and-truck assembly plant of Swedish automaker AB Volvo in Wroclaw in western Poland, Shuter said.
The region's booming demand for new autos also is generating freight business for spare parts needed for repairs and service.
New auto sales rose nearly 40 percent to 842,565 units in the Central European Free Trade Agreement countries of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
"The requirements for automakers and dealers to serve the spare-parts market are demanding because customers increasingly believe that they should not have to wait for parts," he said.
"And a greater proportion of this kind of freight will go by air because companies like GM are placing a hugh emphasis on customer service."
